hints: Start by writing the link between dissolving and energies as $\Delta H_{sol} = \Delta H_{hyd} - \Delta H_{latt}$ and think which two energies control solubility.
Consider what happens to ionic radius of $\text{M}^{2+}$ down Group 2 and how charge density affects attraction to both lattice ions and water molecules.
Compare the size of the change in $\Delta H_{latt}$ with the size of the change in $\Delta H_{hyd}$ when the anion $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is very large.
walkthrough:
Picture dissolving as two energy steps**
Think of dissolving $\text{MSO}_4$ as first breaking the lattice apart, which costs energy, then hydrating the separated $\text{M}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions, which releases energy. The balance is $\Delta H_{sol} = \Delta H_{hyd} - \Delta H_{latt}$. If the overall balance becomes more positive, dissolving is less favoured.

Track ionic size down the group**
Going from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ the cation gets larger, so charge density falls. A lower charge density weakens attraction both in the solid lattice and to water molecules in hydration. So both lattice formation and hydration become less exothermic.

Decide which effect wins for a large anion**
Here the anion $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is large compared to the cations. Changing the cation size has only a small proportional effect on the cation-anion distance in the lattice, so $\Delta H_{latt}$ falls only slightly. For hydration, the small highly charging $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is hydrated very strongly, while large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is hydrated much more weakly, so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ falls steeply. Hydration dominates.

Link to solubility**
Because the exothermic hydration term is lost faster than the lattice cost is saved, $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes less negative and then more positive down the group. A more endothermic solution enthalpy means less soluble sulfates.

Final answer: Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic / less negative down the group.
$\Delta H_{latt}$ changes by a smaller extent while $\Delta H_{hyd}$ changes by a larger extent and is dominant.
Therefore $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes less exothermic / more endothermic, so solubility decreases.

hints: Recall what gas is always produced when a Group 2 metal reacts with dilute acid, then use part (a) to predict whether $\text{MgSO}_4$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$ stay in solution.
walkthrough:
Separate gas evolution from precipitate**
Both metals are oxidised by $\text{H}^+$ to give $\text{H}_2$ gas, so you see fizzing in both tubes: $\text{M} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{MSO}_4 + \text{H}_2$. The difference is the sulfate product. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble so the solution stays colourless, while $\text{BaSO}_4$ is very insoluble so a white solid coats the barium and appears as a precipitate.

Final answer: magnesium: fizzing / effervescence due to $\text{H}_2$.
barium: fizzing and white solid / white precipitate of $\text{BaSO}_4$ forms.

hints: Write the dissolving equilibrium $\text{BaSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$ and express $K_{sp}$ in terms of solubility $s$ in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
Plan the unit conversion from $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ to g per $100 \text{ cm}^3$ using $M_r(\text{BaSO}_4)=233.4$ and $100 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.1 \text{ dm}^3$.
walkthrough:
Get molar solubility from Ksp**
Let $s$ be solubility in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Then $[\text{Ba}^{2+}]=s$ and $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}]=s$, so: $$K_{sp} = s^2$$ $$s = \sqrt{1.08 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.04 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Convert to mass per 100 cm3**
Multiply by molar mass to get g per $\text{dm}^3$, then divide by 10 because $100 \text{ cm}^3$ is one tenth of a $\text{dm}^3$: $$1.04 \times 10^{-5} \times 233.4 = 2.43 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g dm}^{-3}$$ $$2.43 \times 10^{-3} / 10 = 2.43 \times 10^{-4} \text{ g per } 100 \text{ cm}^3$$ This tiny value confirms $\text{BaSO}_4$ is effectively insoluble.

Final answer: solubility $= \sqrt{1.08 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.04 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$= 1.04 \times 10^{-5} \times 233.4 / 10 = 2.43 \times 10^{-4}$ g per $100 \text{ cm}^3$ of solution

hints: Sketch a Born-Haber cycle for $\text{BaSO}_4$ with the formation route at the bottom and the atomisation plus ionisation plus gaseous ion formation route at the top.
Identify which five Table 1.1 values are needed to reach $\text{Ba}^{2+}(g) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(g)$ and then form the lattice, ignoring the sulfur and oxygen atomisation rows.
Set $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{BaSO}_4)$ equal to the sum of the cycle steps and solve for the unknown $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{SO}_4^{2-}(g))$.
walkthrough:
Build the correct cycle**
Start from elements $\text{Ba}(s) + \text{S}(s) + 2\text{O}_2(g)$. One path goes directly to $\text{BaSO}_4(s)$ with $\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = -1473 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. The indirect path goes via $\text{Ba}(g)$ ($+180$), $\text{Ba}^{2+}(g)$ ($+503 +965$), $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(g)$ (unknown $X$), then lattice formation $\text{Ba}^{2+}(g) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(g) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$ ($-2469$).

Apply Hess law**
Both routes start and end at the same points, so: $$\Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{BaSO}_4) = \Delta H_{at}(\text{Ba}) + IE_1 + IE_2 + X + \Delta H_{latt}$$ $$-1473 = 180 + 503 + 965 + X - 2469$$ Note the sulfur atomisation, $\text{S}(g) \rightarrow \text{S}^{2-}(g)$, $\text{O}(g) \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}(g)$ and $\text{O=O}$ bond data are distractors because $X$ already bundles $\text{S}(s) + 2\text{O}_2(g) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{SO}_4^{2-}(g)$.

Solve for the unknown**
Rearrange: $$X = -1473 -180 -503 -965 +2469 = -652 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign makes sense because bringing $\text{S}$, $\text{O}_2$ and electrons together to form the polyatomic ion is overall exothermic.

Final answer: $-1473 = 180 + 503 + 965 + \Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{SO}_4^{2-}(g)) - 2469$
$\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(g) = -652 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Compare the charges of $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cs}^+$ and recall how lattice energy depends on ionic charge.
Compare ionic sizes and think how charge density controls the electrostatic attraction to $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
Use charge and size to judge strength**
Lattice energy is proportional to charge product divided by ion separation. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ carries a $2+$ charge versus $1+$ for $\text{Cs}^+$, and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is also smaller than the large $\text{Cs}^+$ ion. Higher charge and shorter distance both strengthen electrostatic attraction.

State the comparison**
Stronger attraction means more energy is released when the gaseous ions pack into a lattice, so formation of $\text{BaSO}_4(s)$ from $\text{Ba}^{2+}(g) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(g)$ is more exothermic than formation of $\text{Cs}_2\text{SO}_4(s)$ from its gaseous ions.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{latt}$ of $\text{BaSO}_4$ is more negative / larger in magnitude than that of $\text{Cs}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Because $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Cs}^+$ and / or has a larger charge, giving stronger attraction between oppositely charged ions.

hints: Recall the feasibility condition $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus} \le 0$ and set $\Delta G^{\ominus}=0$ for the minimum temperature.
Check units carefully by converting $\Delta S^{\ominus}=+616 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ to $\text{kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ before dividing, then convert K to $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
Set Gibbs energy to zero**
Feasibility begins when $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ just becomes negative. At the boundary: $$0 = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$ $$T = \Delta H^{\ominus} / \Delta S^{\ominus}$$ This works because the reaction is endothermic ($+132 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$) but entropy driven ($+616 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ due to gas and liquid formation).

Calculate and convert**
Convert entropy: $616 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1} = 0.616 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$. Then: $$T = 132 / 0.616 = 214.3 \text{ K}$$ $$T \text{ in } ^{\circ}\text{C} = 214.3 - 273.15 = -58.9 ^{\circ}\text{C}$$ So above about $-59 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ the $T\Delta S$ term outweighs $\Delta H$ and the reaction is feasible.

Final answer: At minimum $T$, $\Delta G^{\ominus}=0$, so $T = \Delta H^{\ominus} / \Delta S^{\ominus}$
$T = 132 / 0.616 = 214 \text{ K} = -59 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ (accept $-58.7 ^{\circ}\text{C}$)

hints: Write $\Delta S^{\ominus} = \Sigma S^{\ominus}(products) - \Sigma S^{\ominus}(reactants)$ and multiply each Table 1.2 value by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Recall $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$ and convert $T=25 ^{\circ}\text{C}$ to 298 K with $\Delta S$ in $\text{kJ K}^{-1}$.
Use the sign of $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ to explain why this reaction proceeds at room temperature while the nitrate reaction in (e)(i) needs warming.
walkthrough:
Sum entropies with stoichiometry**
Products: $2\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{BaCl}_2\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. Reactants: $\text{Ba(OH)}_2\cdot8\text{H}_2\text{O}(s) + 2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$. So: $$\Delta S^{\ominus} = [2(192) + 203 + 8(70)] - [427 + 2(95)]$$ $$= [384 + 203 + 560] - [427 + 190] = 1147 - 617 = +530 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$ The large positive value reflects formation of gas and many moles of liquid from solids.

Insert into Gibbs equation**
At $25 ^{\circ}\text{C}$, $T = 298 \text{ K}$ and $\Delta H^{\ominus}=+133 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$$ $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 133 - 298 \times 0.530$$

Evaluate and interpret**
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 133 - 157.9 = -24.9 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ A negative $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ means the reaction is feasible at 298 K, which is why mixing $\text{Ba(OH)}_2\cdot8\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ fizzes spontaneously and feels very cold as it absorbs heat.

Final answer: $\Delta S^{\ominus} = (203 + (70 \times 8) + (2 \times 192)) - (427 + (2 \times 95)) = +530 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus} = 133 - (298 \times 0.530) = -24.9 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
